parsed.gloss: reḳhte ke = of Rekhta (the old name for Urdu poetry); tumhīñ = you alone/only you; ustād = master/expert; nahīñ ho = are not; 'ġhālib' = Ghalib (pen name, also means 'dominant/victor'); kahte haiñ = they say; agle zamāne meñ = in the former age/earlier time; koī = someone/some; 'mīr' = Mir (Mir Taqi Mir, the great predecessor poet; also means 'leader/chief'); bhī = also/even; thā = was
parsed.literal:
Of Rekhta, you alone are not the master, Ghalib—
They say in the earlier age there was also someone called Mir.
parsed.poetic:
You are not the only master of Rekhta, Ghalib—
They say in times gone by there was also one Mir.
notes: Rekhta is the older term for Urdu poetry, specifically the mixed Persian-Urdu poetic idiom; using it signals the classical tradition Ghalib is being measured against.
The pen name 'Ghalib' means 'dominant' or 'victor' — the couplet ironically undercuts the boast implicit in the name by reminding him of a predecessor.
Mir Taqi Mir (1723–1810) was the great Urdu ghazal poet of the previous generation, often called 'Khuda-e Sukhan' (God of Poetry). Ghalib himself acknowledged Mir's greatness.
The word 'mīr' also means 'leader' or 'chief', so the line works doubly: there was a poet named Mir, and there was a 'chief' of poetry before you.
The address to himself in the third person using his pen name is a standard ghazal convention (takhallus), here used for self-irony rather than self-praise.
The tone is wry and self-deprecating on the surface, but it also asserts Ghalib's own standing by placing him in direct comparison with Mir — only a true master could be addressed this way.
parsed.lost: The double meaning of 'mīr' as both a proper name and a title of rank ('chief/leader') cannot be carried into English. The resonance of 'Rekhta' as the old name for Urdu poetry, with its historical and cultural weight, is flattened in translation. The pen name 'Ghalib' meaning 'victor' creates an irony that English readers miss. The cultural shorthand of invoking Mir — for Urdu readers, the equivalent of saying 'there was also a Shakespeare' — requires explanation rather than landing instantly.

parsed.gloss: haiñ aur bhī = there are also others; duniyā meñ = in the world; suḳhan-var = eloquent speakers / poets; bahut achchhe = very good / excellent; kahte haiñ = they say; ki = that; 'ġhālib' kā = of Ghalib; hai = is; andāz-e-bayāñ = style of expression / manner of speech; aur = different / other / unique
parsed.literal:
There are also many other very good poets in the world;
they say that Ghalib's style of expression is different.
parsed.poetic:
The world holds many a fine poet besides —
but Ghalib's voice, they say, is of another kind.
notes: The pen name 'Ghalib' appears in the second line, as required by the ghazal convention of takhallus (poetic signature) in the maqta (final couplet).

The word 'aur' (other/different) is the entire punch of the couplet — it is deliberately understated. Ghalib does not say 'better', only 'different', but the implication of uniqueness and superiority is unmistakable. I rendered this as 'of another kind' to preserve the understated boast.
'Sukhan-var' literally means 'one who possesses speech/eloquence' — a stock term for poets in the classical tradition. I used 'poet' in the literal and 'fine poet' in the poetic version.

'Andāz-e-bayāñ' (style of expression) is a key aesthetic term in Urdu poetics, referring to a poet's distinctive manner or idiom. I kept 'style of expression' in the literal and shifted to 'voice' in the poetic rendering for naturalness.
The couplet is an ironic self-praise disguised as reported speech ('they say'), a common Ghalibian move — the modesty of the first line sets up the quiet boast of the second.
parsed.lost: The full force of 'aur' as a single-word understatement — in Urdu it lands with immense weight precisely because it is so minimal; English needs more words to convey the same implication. Also lost is the cultural resonance of the takhallus 'Ghalib' (meaning 'conqueror' or 'dominant'), which adds a layer of wordplay: the poet named 'Conqueror' conquers through sheer difference of style.

parsed.literal:
The world is a children's playground before me
Night and day a spectacle keeps happening before me
parsed.poetic:
The world before me is a child's plaything,
A spectacle unceasing spread before me.
notes: bāzīcha-e-atfāl literally means 'plaything of children' — the earth as a toy or game that children play with, implying its impermanence and triviality from the speaker's elevated perspective.

mire aage has a double sense: spatial (before my eyes) and temporal (ahead of my life / still to come), and can also carry the Sufi connotation of 'in the presence of my true self or God-consciousness'.

tamāshā is a key Mughal-era word: it means spectacle, entertainment, show — often used for public performances or curiosities. Here it suggests the world's affairs are a passing show watched with detachment.
shab-o-roz (night and day) is an idiom for 'constantly / ceaselessly'.
The repeated 'mire aage' at the end of both lines works as a refrain-like stress, which I kept by ending both English lines with 'before me'.
Ghalib is not using his pen name (takhallus) in this two-line selection; it is not the closing couplet of the ghazal.
parsed.lost: The Persianate resonance of 'bāzīcha' (toy/plaything) as a word for the world's triviality — English 'plaything' captures the sense but not the classical literary weight. 'Tamāshā' has a rich cultural range — spectacle, entertainment, curiosity, mockery — that 'spectacle' only partially conveys. The grammatical compactness of the Urdu, where 'hotā hai' implies ongoing, habitual unfolding of the show, flattens somewhat in English.

parsed.gloss: bas-ki: to such an extent / so much so that; dushvār: difficult; har kaam kā āsāñ honā: the becoming easy of every task; aadmī: man, human being (literally 'son of Adam'); ko bhī: even for; mayassar nahīñ: not attainable/available; insāñ honā: becoming human / attaining true humanity
parsed.literal:
So difficult is the becoming easy of every task
Even for man, becoming human is not attainable
parsed.poetic:
So hard is it for any task to become easy—
even a man cannot attain to being truly human.
notes: The central wordplay is aadmī versus insāñ: both can mean 'man/human,' but aadmī suggests the ordinary biological or social human (literally 'son of Adam'), while insāñ carries moral and Sufi overtones of true, perfected humanity.
The first line's paradox—difficulty of ease—sets up the second line's paradox: a human failing to become truly human.
bas-ki works as an intensifier meaning 'to such an extent that,' making the second line a consequence of the first.
mayassar implies something granted or made available, not merely possible by effort, which suits the spiritual register.
The verbal noun honā can mean 'being' or 'becoming'; I use 'becoming' to emphasize the movement from aadmī to insāñ.
parsed.lost: English cannot fully reproduce the aadmī/insāñ distinction with two equally common words; 'man' versus 'truly human' is a partial solution but loses the compact moral-spiritual weight of insāñ. The Persianate noun phrase 'har kaam kā āsāñ honā' also becomes more abstract or wordy in English.

Leaf by leaf, plant by plant, knows our condition.

Each leaf, each sprig, knows my plight.

The phrase jaane na jaane ... hī na jaane sets up a concessive contrast: even if the beloved/rose is ignorant or indifferent, the rest of creation is not.

parsed.literal:
When nothing was, God was; if nothing were, God would be.
Being drowned me; if I were not, then what would be?
parsed.poetic:
When nothing was, God was; if nothing were, God would be.
Being has drowned me; had I not been, what would there be?
notes: The first line uses a conditional/correlative structure to assert God's necessary existence independent of all contingent things.
The repeated forms of honā (thā, hotā, hotā, hone, hotā, hotā) create a dense philosophical wordplay on being, existence, and non-existence.
Duboyā literally means 'drowned'; I keep the water image in the poetic version because it is vivid, though idiomatically it means 'ruined/undid me.'
Hone ne personifies being/existence as the agent that drowns the speaker—existence itself is the calamity.
The final kyā hotā is deliberately ambiguous: it can mean 'what would exist?', 'what would happen?', or 'what would it matter?' I chose 'what would there be?' to keep the existential question open.
The sher has no pen-name (takhallus) in this couplet, so none is rendered.
parsed.lost: English cannot carry the compact repetition and polyptoton of honā (thā/hotā/hone) that makes the paradox of being and non-being feel like a single unfolding argument. The final ambiguity of kyā hotā—between 'what would exist,' 'what would happen,' and 'what would it matter'—also cannot be preserved in one English phrase.

parsed.literal:
Iqbal is not despairing of his barren field;
if it gets a little moisture, then this soil is very fertile, O cup-bearer.
parsed.poetic:
Iqbal is not hopeless of his field gone bare—
Just wet this earth a little, cup-bearer; it is rich beyond compare.
notes: kisht-e-vīrāñ (barren field) is a stock metaphor for a person, nation, or spiritual state that has become unproductive; Iqbal uses it for the Muslim ummah or the self.
zarḳhez (fertile) is the key contrast: the soil's potential richness is latent, awaiting only 'nam' (moisture).
nam (moisture) carries a double sense: literal water for the field, and wine or spiritual grace (faiz) in the Sufi register—hence the address to the saaqī.

saaqī as addressee is a ghazal convention: the wine-pourer / cup-bearer who can also stand for God, the spiritual guide, or the beloved. Here the moisture and fertility metaphor makes 'saaqī' function as one who waters rather than pours wine.
The pen name 'Iqbal' embedded in line one is the maqt'a convention; the poet speaks about himself in the third person.
parsed.lost: The double resonance of 'nam' as both water and wine, and 'saaqī' as both cup-bearer and waterer/rain-giver, is compressed in English. The rapid syllabic music of 'zarā nam ho to ye miTTī bahut zarḳhez hai saaqī' cannot be reproduced, nor the rhyme/internal echo of 'vīrāñ' with 'zarḳhez' as land-states.

A sigh needs a whole lifetime to take effect—

notes: The beloved’s zulf (long, curling, tangled tresses) is a stock ghazal image of endless beauty and entrapment; its tip or end (sar) is always receding.
The first line treats the lover’s aah as slow-acting: it only produces asar (effect) after a lifetime.
The original ends both lines with hote tak, creating a rhythmic echo, and plays on the sonic and visual closeness of asar (effect) and sar (tip/end/head).
kaun jiitā hai is a rhetorical question: ‘who lives long enough?’ implies no one can.
I rendered sar as ‘end/tip’ to preserve the impossible-distance image, but had to sacrifice its literal sense of ‘head’.
parsed.lost: The asar/sar wordplay, the repetition of hote tak, and the full symbolic resonance of aah and zulf in the Urdu ghazal tradition cannot be fully carried into English.

parsed.gloss: huuñ maiñ parvāna = I am a moth; magar = but; sham.a = candle/flame; to ho = there should be; raat = night; to ho = there should be; jaan dené ko = to give my life; huuñ maujūd = I am present/ready; koī baat = some matter/occasion/thing; to ho = there should be
parsed.literal:
I am a moth, but there should be a candle, there should be a night
I am present to give my life — there should be some occasion
parsed.poetic:
A moth I am — but let there be a flame, a night,
I stand ready to die — let there be some cause, some rite.
notes: Parvāna (moth) and sham.a (candle) are stock ghazal symbols: the moth circles the flame and immolates itself, representing the lover's willing self-destruction for the beloved.
The repeated 'to ho' (there should be / let there be) creates a conditional, almost playful tone — the speaker is eager but insists on the proper setting or pretext.

'koī baat to ho' carries a double sense: 'some occasion/cause' and colloquially 'let there be something special/remarkable about it.' I rendered this as 'some cause, some rite' to keep both the occasion and the ceremonial weight.

The couplet subverts the usual ghazal trope: instead of the moth being helplessly drawn to the flame, here the moth is ready and waiting, but the flame and night are missing — a witty, almost comic inversion.
Akbar Allahabadi's signature irony is present: the lover's grand gesture of self-sacrifice is undercut by the mundane condition that the setting must first exist.
parsed.lost: The colloquial punch of 'koī baat to ho' — which in everyday Urdu means 'there should be something to it' or 'it should be worth it' — is only partially captured by 'some cause, some rite.' The rhythmic insistence of the triple 'to ho' is also difficult to reproduce in English without sounding mechanical.

parsed.literal:
What a fine veil/screen it is: they sit pressed against the curtain—
plainly they neither hide, nor come forward into view.
parsed.poetic:
An excellent veil indeed—they sit close to the screen,
plainly neither hidden, nor plainly to be seen.
notes: parda means both a physical veil/curtain and the cultural institution of purdah/seclusion; chilman is a split-bamboo screen, giving the scene a domestic, flirtatious intimacy.

sāmne ānā idiomatically means 'to come before someone / appear'; I rendered it as 'to be seen' to keep the paradox and rhyme.

parsed.gloss: ham: I/we (the lover); aah bhī karte haiñ: even (if) I/we sigh; to: then; ho jaate haiñ badnām: become disgraced, ill-famed; vo: that one, the beloved/he/she; qatl bhī karte haiñ: even (if) commits murder; to: then; charchā nahīñ hotā: no talk/gossip/scandal arises
parsed.literal:
If I even sigh, I become disgraced.
If she even commits murder, no talk arises.
parsed.poetic:
A sigh from me, and I am disgraced;
she commits murder, and not a whisper rises.
notes: The whole couplet turns on the parallel use of 'bhī' in both lines: even the lover's smallest act, a sigh, brings disgrace, while even the beloved's greatest act, murder, brings no public censure.
'aah' is a stock ghazal symbol: the lover's involuntary sigh of pain or longing, sometimes also understood as a curse. I translated it simply as 'sigh' to keep the intimate register.
'qatl' here is metaphorical murder: the beloved kills the lover through beauty, indifference, or cruelty, not literal bloodshed.

'badnām' and 'charchā' are both terms of public reputation, but they are not synonyms. 'badnām' means disgraced or ill-famed; 'charchā' means talk, mention, or gossip. The beloved's killing does not even become a topic of conversation.

The pronouns 'ham' and 'vo' are ambiguous. 'ham' can be singular or plural, and 'vo' can be he, she, or they; in the ghazal tradition 'vo' usually points to the beloved or even the Divine. I used 'I' and 'she' to follow the conventional English ghazal idiom.
This couplet does not contain the poet's pen name, so no takhallus appears here.
parsed.lost: English cannot fully carry the exact parallelism of 'bhī...to' in both lines, the gender ambiguity of 'vo', the multiple resonances of 'aah' and 'qatl' within Sufi and erotic registers, or the precise social contrast between being 'badnām' and not even being the subject of 'charchā'.

parsed.literal:
All the plans were turned upside down; the medicine did no work.
I saw: this sickness of the heart at last did the work completely.
parsed.poetic:
All plans went awry; the remedy had no effect.
Behold, this heart-disease at last finished the job for good.
notes: The first line sets up medical and practical failure: tadbīr (plan/remedy) and davā (medicine) both fail, leaving no cure.
bīmāri-e-dil means both a physical heart disease and the traditional ghazal illness of love and longing; I keep ‘heart-disease’ to preserve both.
kaam tamām kiyā literally means ‘made the work complete’, but as an idiom it can mean to finish someone off or kill. My poetic ‘finished the job for good’ gestures at that idiomatic finality.
The verse repeats kaam (‘work’) in both lines: the medicine could not do its work, while the heart-sickness completed its work. This contrast is kept in the literal and echoed in the poetic.
parsed.lost: The exact echo of kaam kiyā / kaam tamām kiyā is not as compact in English, and the idiom ‘to make an end of someone’ is only partly carried by ‘finish the job’. English also cannot keep the resonance of dil as both the physical organ and the seat of love in a single unmarked word.

parsed.gloss: aa.e haiñ — have come; mīr — Meer (poet's pen name); kāfir ho kar — having become an infidel/unbeliever; ḳhudā ke ghar meñ — in God's house (mosque/Kaaba/sanctuary); peshānī — forehead; qashqa — sectarian/forehead mark, often associated with Hindu or antinomian identity; zunnār — cord/sacred thread worn by non-Muslims, symbol of infidelity or love in ghazal; kamar — waist.
parsed.literal:
Meer has come, having become an infidel, into God's house.
On his forehead is a qashqa; a zunnar is around his waist.
parsed.poetic:
Meer has come as a kafir into the house of God—
a qashqa on his forehead, a zunnar round his waist.
notes: The pen name 'Meer' is embedded as the subject of the first line, a signature typical of ghazal even when not in the final couplet.

kāfir ho kar is deliberately paradoxical: he enters God's house not as a Muslim but bearing the marks of a religious outsider; in Sufi/antinomian poetry this can be a proud badge of the lover whom orthodoxy rejects.
qashqa and zunnār are paired symbols of non-Muslim identity—forehead mark and waist cord/thread—and by extension of love's 'heresy' or devotion beyond outward law.
The Persianate/Urdu ghazal often uses qashqa and zunnār as the uniform of the qalandar or antinomian lover, making the religious transgression a form of spiritual sincerity.
I kept qashqa and zunnār in the poetic translation because English equivalents such as 'tilak' or 'sacred thread' narrow or shift the cultural resonance.
parsed.lost: The rhyme and sonic compactness of ghar/kamar with meñ, the specifically Indian/Persian sectarian connotations of qashqa and zunnār, and the double-edged word kāfir as both orthodox accusation and Sufi self-identification cannot be fully carried into English.
